entries.claim: Firewall settings are adjusted by going to Settings, then Sites, clicking on the site, then clicking the Firewall tab.
entries.verbatim: To adjust your firewall settings, go to `Settings`, then `Sites`, click on your site, then click the `Firewall` tab.

entries.claim: The firewall offers separate list tabs for Pages, IPs, Referrers, Domains, Countries, and Events.
entries.verbatim: Open a list tab (Pages, IPs, Referrers, Domains, Countries, or Events).

entries.claim: Blocking pages, IPs, domains, or countries in the firewall does not prevent visitors from accessing or navigating the site; it only prevents their visits from being shown as data in the Fathom dashboard.
entries.verbatim: Note: If you've blocked pages, IPs, domains, or countries, visitors coming from those sources will still be able to access and navigate around your site, but their visits just won't be shown as data in your Fathom dashboard.

entries.claim: Pageviews from blocked pages do not count as pageviews and so do not count against the customer's payment plan allotment of pageviews.
entries.verbatim: Visitors who visit blocked pages do not count as pageviews, so they do not count against your payment plan allotment of pageviews.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics firewall - blocked pages
context.conditions: Applies to pages blocked via the firewall's Pages list.

entries.claim: Currently, only IPv4 addresses are supported for wildcard IP blocking in the firewall.
entries.verbatim: **Note:** Currently only IPv4 addresses are supported for wildcards

context.subject: Fathom Analytics firewall IP blocking
context.conditions: Applies to wildcard IP entries only.
context.limitations: IPv6 wildcard support not stated.

entries.claim: Once one or more allowed domains are added to the firewall's Domains list, data from any other domain is blocked instantly.
entries.verbatim: **Once you add one or more allowed domains, this means data coming from any other domain will be blocked instantly**.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics firewall domain allow list

entries.claim: In the Events firewall tab, Block drops the specified event names while still collecting every other event, Allow collects only the listed names and wildcard patterns, and an empty allow list collects every event.
entries.verbatim: **Block** drops those names and still collects every other event. **Allow** collects only the names (and wildcard patterns) on the list. An empty allow list collects every event.

entries.claim: The firewall only stops future visits; existing spam already recorded in reports must be removed separately using Data removals in the site's Manage settings.
entries.verbatim: The firewall stops future visits. To clean up spam that’s already in your reports, use `Data removals` in your site’s `Manage` settings.

entries.claim: An empty firewall list does not filter any traffic.
entries.verbatim: Choose `Block` or `Allow` the following values, then add them. An empty list does not filter.

objections.objection: Google Analytics is free and does more. Why would I start paying $15 a month for less?
objections.answer: The evidence meets this head-on rather than dodging it: there is deliberately no free plan, and the stated reason is infrastructure investment (E191, E192). The counter-frame is the business model — Fathom says it sells software, not data, and that free analytics are paid for with visitor data (E256, E193, E262, E151). Concretely: entry is $15/month for up to 100,000 pageviews across 50 sites (E157, E257), yearly billing gives two months free (E168), and the trial can run alongside Google Analytics so the comparison is empirical rather than rhetorical (E171). What the evidence does not do is claim feature parity with GA4, and copy should not either.

provenance.quote: Nope, and here’s why: we’ve invested heavily in fast, reliable infrastructure (we don’t host Fathom on cheap servers that go offline).

objections.objection: Switching means abandoning years of history, and I will lose the ability to compare this year with last year.
objections.answer: GA4 history can be imported, with no extra charge for historical imports, and the import is an authorise-select-run flow rather than a Google Cloud API key exercise (E42, E243, E74, E140). Imported history stays viewable and exportable while subscribed (E43), and Fathom's own retention is open-ended — data back to signup day for as long as you are a customer (E229, E69, E248, E145). Two honest limits belong in the same breath: the importer does not recreate every GA4 report and does not bring events (E44), and Universal Analytics data is gone because Google deleted it in July 2024 (E47).

objections.objection: The imported numbers will not match what Google showed me, so I will end up trusting neither tool.
objections.answer: Partially answerable, and only by saying it first: Fathom's own documentation states imported data has different filtering options and that totals can differ between tools (E45), and that large imports may need smaller date ranges (E46). The resolution on offer is parallel running during the trial so the reader calibrates the gap themselves rather than discovering it after switching (E171, E242), plus the reasons Fathom's counts differ by design — bot and crawler filtering (E122, E178) and no cookies or sampling-driven blind spots (E221, E90). There is no reconciliation report or mapping in the evidence.

provenance.quote: Imported data has different filtering options from data collected by Fathom, and the totals can differ between tools.

objections.objection: A single-page dashboard is too thin for how I work — I need funnels, cohorts, user-level paths, attribution across sessions and custom report building.
objections.answer: Nothing in the supplied evidence answers this, and that is the finding. The ceiling is explicit: one page of data (E76, E53) covering live and total visitors, pageviews, top pages, referrers, countries, devices, browsers, events and UTM campaigns, with filters, saved views, milestones and date comparisons. There is no funnel, cohort, session-path, multi-touch attribution or report-builder capability anywhere in the ledger, and Fathom frames the absence as the product's point rather than a roadmap gap. A reader who genuinely needs those should be allowed to disqualify themselves early; the Analytics API and CSV export (E179, E138, E139) are the only partial escape hatch, and they shift work onto the reader.

objections.objection: Seven days with my card on file is not long enough to judge an analytics tool, and I will forget to cancel.
objections.answer: The trial terms are documented and unusually explicit: card required, not charged until the trial ends, an email before billing starts, cancel anytime in account settings with no contracts and no call required (E170, E171, E185). Every plan includes the same features during the trial, so nothing is withheld (E169). Evaluation does not have to depend on the seven days alone — an eight-to-ten minute dashboard walkthrough and a clickable live demo exist without signing up (E190, E78, cta-live-demo), and the trial is designed to run alongside existing analytics (E171). Note the real residue: seven days of a low-traffic site is still a small sample, and nothing in the evidence extends it.

provenance.quote: Choose a plan and add your card to start a 7-day free trial. Your card is not charged until the trial ends, and we’ll email you before your plan starts billing. Your subscription then renews automatically unless you cancel in your account settings. You can run Fathom alongside your existing analytics while you try it.

objections.objection: Installing it means touching production templates and adding another script to a page I have spent weeks making fast.
objections.answer: Installation is one line of JavaScript in the header with the site's Site ID (E24, E242, E143, E27), or no template edits at all via the WordPress plugin and the other integrations — Ghost, Webflow, Next, Nuxt, Vue, Drupal, Carrd and more (E16, E103, E142, E244). Performance: a few KB, deferred and asynchronous, served from the nearest CDN edge, stated not to hurt PageSpeed (E80, E144, E222). Removing the cookie consent manager is itself a page-weight saving (E86, E227). Install can be confirmed in seconds by watching the Realtime count (E17), and staging or local traffic can be kept out via allowed domains, an IP filter or a browser-level block (E19, E20, E21, E22, E23).

objections.objection: Our security policy or hosting requirements mean we need to self-host analytics, or at minimum keep all data on our own infrastructure.
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence answers this objection — it is a disqualifier. The documentation states plainly that Fathom is a hosted product only, with the trade-off being global CDN processing, fast dashboards and EU processing of EU visitor data. Copy should not attempt to argue around it; the nearest adjacent comfort available (EU routing, privacy-lawyer review, named enterprise logos) addresses data residency, not self-hosting, and a buyer whose constraint is literally on-premise will read any such pivot as evasion.

provenance.quote: No. Fathom is a hosted product so we can process pageviews on a global CDN, keep dashboards fast, and process EU visitor data in the EU.

objections.objection: I cannot get this past my team or procurement without a demo, a security review and someone on a call — and they explicitly do not do sales calls.
objections.answer: Only partly answerable. Fathom states outright that it does no sales calls or live demos, offering instead a ten-minute walkthrough video, a clickable live dashboard and the trial (E190), plus email support from real humans on every plan (E181, cta-contact-support). For internal credibility: privacy lawyers have vetted collection and storage (E120), EU traffic routes through European-owned infrastructure under Canada's EU adequacy decision (E219, E34), compliance with GDPR, ePrivacy, PECR and CCPA is claimed (E116-E119, E220), and the customer base is described as including Fortune 100s, banks, governments and Premier League clubs, with named logos (E230, E258, E231). Be precise about what is missing: no named certifying body, no audit report, no SOC 2 or ISO reference anywhere in the evidence, and the logos are logo placements with no usage detail. A procurement process that requires an attestation will not be satisfied by this material.

provenance.quote: We don’t do sales calls or live demos, but our software is ridiculously easy to use. You can watch our [10-minute walkthrough](/video/dashboard-walkthrough), click around the [live dashboard](https://app.usefathom.com/demo) or give Fathom a 7-day free trial alongside your existing analytics.

objections.objection: If I am leaving Google anyway, Cloudflare's analytics are free and I could self-host Matomo or Plausible — why pay this one?
objections.answer: The evidence engages this as a comparison rather than denying it. Cloudflare's privacy-first analytics are acknowledged as free (E99, E100); the counter is paid-product consequences, not feature claims. Against Matomo specifically: cloud retention capped at 24 months versus retention for as long as you are a customer (E68, E69); cookies and consent notices unless several steps are taken correctly, versus anonymisation and no cookies by default (E87, E88, E89, E90, E91, E92, E66); a GA import needing a Google Cloud API key versus a button (E73, E74); a 20-50KB script you must put behind your own CDN versus a few KB on Fathom's (E82, E83, E80); 12 sections and 70+ reports versus one page (E75, E76). Against self-hosting generally, Fathom's position is that it is hosted so there is no infrastructure to run (E148, E192). All of the Matomo points are Fathom's own comparison claims, not independent verification (E60, E63, E68), and must be attributed as such.

provenance.quote: They offer privacy-first, lightweight and simple website analytics—and their analytics are free.

objections.objection: My traffic is spiky. One post that takes off and I am either throttled, surprise-billed or forced up a tier I do not need the rest of the year.
objections.answer: Documented and generous: occasional spikes are never charged for and the account is not shut off on hitting the limit early (E253); staying well over the limit triggers an email about a larger plan with the decision left to the customer, friendly reminders and extra time before dashboard and API access pauses, and data keeps being collected throughout (E186, E254, E255). Downgrading is self-serve after two consecutive months under the tier (E189). Quota hygiene is in the customer's hands: blocked pages and excluded local, staging or test environments do not count against the allotment (E10, E18), and bots are filtered automatically (E122, E178). Two caveats to state rather than hide: custom events count against the same monthly allowance (E187, E183), and sites on one plan share it (E247).

provenance.quote: We’ll never turn your analytics off for occasional traffic spikes. If you stay well over your limit, we’ll email you about a larger plan, and you decide whether to upgrade or cancel (no hard feelings either way). We send a few friendly reminders and extra time before we pause dashboard and API access, and we keep collecting your data throughout.

objections.objection: It is two bootstrapped founders with no funding. If they fold or get acquired, my analytics history goes with them.
objections.answer: Thinly answerable. Independence is stated as a feature — no venture capital, bank loans or outside shareholders, and pricing set to be sustainable because the business model is software rather than data (E245, E193, E256); the company has been running since 2018 (E61, E101). Data is exportable at any time as CSV or through the API, and Fathom tells customers to export before cancelling because cancellation queues data for deletion (E138, E139, E250, E70, E185). What the evidence does not contain: revenue, headcount, uptime history or any continuity commitment, and 'thousands of companies' and the logo wall are unquantified vendor statements (E213, E215, E231). Do not dress bootstrapped independence up as a durability guarantee.

profiles.name: Plausible Analytics
profiles.why: Both Plausible and Fathom position themselves as privacy-first, cookieless Google Analytics alternatives with a built-in GA import path—Plausible says 'You can even import your Google Analytics stats' while Fathom's importer requires only authorizing the account, selecting sites and running the import (E74). Plausible markets itself as explicitly EU-hosted, with visitor data processed 'exclusively on servers owned and operated by European companies,' whereas Fathom instead claims its 'intelligent routing' makes its script load 'up to 50% faster than EU-only infrastructure' (E105), treating EU-only hosting as a benchmark to beat rather than a selling point in itself.

Annual billing offers 2 months free versus monthly billing.
profiles.free_entry: 30-day free trial, no credit card required (https://plausible.io/); open-source code available on GitHub.
